abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The bluish‐white appearance of some plants, known as glaucousness, results from the scattering effect of visible light due to plant surface waxes. This adaptive trait can contribute to tolerance of abiotic stresses in wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) such as drought, solar radiation, and heat. In this study, we identified quantitative trait loci (QTLs) and marker‐trait associations for flag leaf and spike glaucousness in two biparental populations and a panel of elite winter wheat lines. For all populations, spike and flag leaf glaucousness were visually scored on a 0–4 scale in multiple environments. Our QTL analyses and association mapping identified a significant locus on the long arm of chromosome 3A (QFlg.ncb‐3A) in all populations, explaining up to 36.6 percent of phenotypic variation for flag leaf glaucousness. Further, in one biparental population we identified three QTLs associated with spike glaucousness, located on chromosomes 1B, 2A, and 4D (QSpg.ncb‐1B, QSpg.ncb‐2A, QSpg.ncb‐4D) where they explained up to 22.8, 20.7, and 14.2 phenotypic variation, respectively. The QSpg.ncb‐1B QTL is located within the t1RS·1BL translocation from rye (Secale cereale L.) and demonstrates how glaucousness variation can be associated with an alien introgression in wheat. Our results suggest that QFlg.ncb‐3A is a primary determinant of flag leaf and, to a lesser extent, spike glaucousness in the evaluated germplasm. Collectively, our results expand the understanding of the genetic control of glaucousness in wheat flag leaf and spikes tissues, suggesting both unique and shared loci may underly the degree of glaucousness on the different plant parts.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Wheat is a staple crop, providing approximately 20% of daily calories and protein for 4.5 billion people worldwide (Shiferaw et al., 2013). Climate change is predicted to alter the distribution of productive agricultural areas, requiring crop improvement to maintain wheat production (Anderson et al., 2020). Drought and heat stress often co‐occur, and the combination of these types of stress causes more significant yield reductions than each stress alone (Anderson et al., 2020; Hussain et al., 2019).

Glaucousness is a bluish‐white coloration found on some plants, resulting from the accumulation of epicuticular wax crystalloids on aerial plant surfaces. Frequently observed in wheat and other plants in the Triticeae tribe, glaucous wax crystalloids form in the presence of β‐diketone aliphatics on the surface waxes of aerial organs. Glaucousness creates a scattering effect of visible light that increases radiation reflectance, while reducing leaf temperatures and transpiration, thereby enhancing leaf survival under water stress (Huang et al., 2017; Richards et al., 1986). It has been implicated in improved tolerance to both drought and heat stresses (Richards et al., 1986; Shaheenuzzamn et al., 2021). Thus, increased glaucousness may be a climate‐adaptive trait, particularly in hot, dry climates.

Genetic studies in wheat have identified four main loci determining the level of glaucousness in wheat: two wax production loci, Wax 1 (W1) and Wax 2 (W2), and two wax inhibition loci, Inhibitor of wax 1 (Iw1) and Inhibitor of wax 2 (Iw2). W1 and Iw1 are linked and reside on the short arm of chromosome 2B (2BS), whereas W2 and Iw2 are located on the short arm of chromosome 2D (2DS; Tsunewaki & Ebana, 1999). Presence of a single wax production locus, W1 or W2, is sufficient to produce a glaucous phenotype. Both Iw1 and Iw2 are dominant repressors leading to non‐glaucous, or glossy, phenotypes; the presence of either Iw1 or Iw2 is sufficient for inhibition of W1 and/or W2 (Tsunewaki & Ebana, 1999). Iw1 inhibits the formation of β‐diketones and hydroxy‐β‐diketones in the peduncle and flag leaf blade cuticles with no differences in cuticle thickness (Adamski et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2017). Iw1 suppresses W1‐COE, a carboxylesterase‐like protein gene within the W1 gene cluster that is involved in diketone wax synthesis (Huang et al., 2017). The regulatory interaction between Iw1/Iw2 and W1/W2 loci provides an “on–off” switch that controls the glaucousness phenotype, and that can be exploited by breeders for fine‐tuning glaucousness in wheat.

A third glaucousness inhibitor has been identified in wheat, named Inhibitor of Wax 3 (Iw3). Iw3 is unique in tissue specificity of wax regulation only in spikes; it is localized to the short arm of chromosome 1B (Dubcovsky et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2014). Metabolic characterization of the glume glaucousness inhibitor locus found that Iw3 inhibited β‐diketone synthesis while affecting the acyl pathway by promoting production of aldehydes and alkanes (Wang et al., 2014). Iw1 and Iw2 also inhibit β‐diketone synthesis; however, they affect the acyl pathway differently by elevating primary alcohols with no influence on alkanes (Zhang et al., 2013). These metabolic differences suggest that Iw3 employs a different mechanism of suppressing the β‐diketone pathway than Iw1 and Iw2 and provides a unique means for breeders to modify a plant's glaucousness level.

Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping studies have revealed more complex genetic control of the degree of glaucousness, with researchers identifying several additional QTLs (Bennett et al., 2012; Mason et al., 2010). Most significantly, a major QTL on the long arm of chromosome 3A has been identified in studies of Australian and global wheat germplasm (Bennett et al., 2012; Würschum et al., 2020). This QTL was found to have a large influence on flag leaf glaucousness, explaining up to 52% of genetic variance for this trait (Bennett et al., 2012). Recently, a genome‐wide association study (GWAS) of global wheat germplasm identified multiple markers within this 3A chromosome region that had significant trait associations; these marker‐trait associations (MTAs) appear to be unique and may interact epistatically (Würschum et al., 2020). The QTL on the long arm of chromosome 3A is shown to have a significant influence on flag leaf glaucousness in wheat via a potentially complex molecular mechanism.

The objective of this study was to expand our understanding of the genetic control of glaucousness in flag leaf and spike tissues of wheat. To do this, we characterized the genetic control of glaucousness in three winter wheat populations, including a panel of regional elite breeding lines and two biparental mapping populations whose parents differ in both spike and flag leaf glaucousness. One of the biparental populations segregates for the t1RS·1BL translocation from rye (Secale cereale L.), providing an opportunity to study the impact of this alien introgression on glaucousness in wheat. We rated glaucousness separately in spike and flag leaf tissues, enabling distinction in the genetic control of glaucousness in these tissues.

sec.title: Plant materials
sec.p: Three different winter wheat populations were used in this study: two recombinant inbred lines (RILs) biparental mapping populations and a GWAS panel representing the Eastern United States regional winter wheat germplasm. The parents of the RIL mapping populations were awned, semidwarfed, soft red winter (SRW) wheat lines.

The LA96135 × AGS2000 biparental mapping population (hereafter referred to as the LA population) comprised 293 F5‐derived RIL developed from the cross between SRW wheat cultivars LA95135 (PI 655291), with a mildly glaucous phenotype, and AGS2000 (PI 619256), with a highly glaucous phenotype (Figure 1). The LA95135 (CL850643/PIO2548//Coker9877/3/FL302/Coker‐762) line was released by the Louisiana State University in 2009. AGS2000 (PIO2555/PF84301//FL302) was cooperatively developed and released jointly by the University of Georgia and the University of Florida in 2002 (Johnson et al., 2002). AGS2000 carries the t1RS·1BL translocation, where the short arm of rye chromosome 1R is translocated onto the long arm of wheat chromosome 1B.

sec.p: A second biparental mapping population was developed by crossing Hilliard with GA06493‐13LE6 (hereafter referred to as the HG population). Breeding line GA06493‐13LE6 (GA981394‐16/AGS2025//SS8641) was developed at the University of Georgia and is adapted to the Southeastern United States. Hilliard was derived from the cross 25R47/Jamestown at Virginia Tech and is remarkable in its wide adaptation from Ontario to Texas (Griffey et al., 2020). GA06493‐13LE6 is highly glaucous, while Hilliard exhibits only a mild glaucous phenotype (Figure 1). The Hilliard × GA06493‐13LE6 (HG) mapping population includes 332 F5‐derived RIL. Marker data from all 332 lines were used for linkage map construction to maximize resolution of the map. However, only 189 lines had sufficient seed for replicated, multi‐environment trials when phenotyped. Thus, the higher resolution in the map does not translate to higher power in the QTL analysis for this population. A GWAS panel, consisting of 263 elite breeding lines, was used to interrogate glaucousness variation present in modern winter wheat germplasm. The breeding lines were entries in six collaborative breeding nurseries from 2020: Gulf‐Atlantic Wheat Nursery, Mason Dixon, SunWheat, Uniform Bread Wheat, 6‐State Preliminary, and 6‐State Advanced, and represent the phenotypic variation available to growers. Seed of lines grown in the RAL20 environment were harvested and planted at RAL21 for a second year of evaluation. These nurseries contain entries from public breeding programs across the Eastern SRW wheat‐growing region.

sec.title: Field trials
sec.p: The SRW wheat populations were grown at three North Carolina environments: Raleigh, in the state's central piedmont region, for the 2020 and 2021 growing seasons (hereafter referred to as RAL20 and RAL21); and Kinston, in the Eastern Coastal Plain region of the state, during 2021 (hereafter referred to as KIN21). Each population was evaluated at two different growing environments. The LA population and GWAS panel were planted at Raleigh in both years (RAL20 and RAL21). The HG population was grown in 2021 at the Kinston and Raleigh locations (KIN21 and RAL21). Each genotype was planted in a single 1.3‐m head row using approximately 3 g of seed per row and grown under conventional management practices. Two replicated blocks were grown for each population in all environments, and genotypes were randomized within replicates.

For all populations, spike and flag leaf glaucousness were rated for each row at, or shortly after, flowering (Zadoks 60; Zadoks et al., 1974). Glaucousness phenotypes were scored visually using a 0–4 scale, where a 0 rating denotes a “glossy” or waxless/non‐glaucous phenotype, and a 4 rating is a highly glaucous phenotype. The visual classification criteria were different for the spike and flag leaf phenotypes, as the trait manifests differently in the two tissues.

For spike glaucousness, visual ratings were based on the overall density of white glaucous epicuticular wax coating the spike (Figure 1C). A rating of 4 represents spikes most densely covered in glaucous epicuticular wax, while a rating of 1 denotes spikes with a minimal coating of white glaucous wax. Leaf glaucousness was rated based on the spread of white glaucous wax on the abaxial sides of flag leaves (Figure 1D). A rating of 4 was given when the leaf blade was glaucous all the way to the tip; a rating of 1 showed only a slight amount of glaucous wax at the base of the leaf.

sec.title: Genotyping
sec.p: All three populations were genotyped using genotyping by sequencing (GBS) for single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) discovery following the methods detailed in Poland et al. (2012). DNA was isolated from plant tissue collected from 10‐day‐old seedlings using the Sbeadex Plant Maxi Kit (LGC Genomics LLC). Individual libraries were prepared, barcoded, pooled, and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 or NovaSeq instrument. Sample pooling was done with 96 samples per lane on the HiSeq 2500 or with 384 samples per SP1 lane on the NovaSeq. The International Wheat Genome Sequencing Consortium RefSeq Chinese Spring v1.0 assembly was used as a reference genome for SNP calling (https://wheat‐urgi.versailles.inra.fr/Seq‐Repository/Assemblies). The TASSEL5 GBS v2 Pipeline v.5.2.35 was used to align sequencing reads to the reference assembly using the Burrows–Wheeler Aligner v.0.7.12 and subsequently to call SNPs (Glaubitz et al., 2014; Li & Durbin, 2009). SNP data were filtered to retain SNP with ≤20% missing data, ≥5% minor allele frequency (MAF), and ≤10% of heterozygous calls per marker. This resulted in 30,519 SNP used in the GWAS. After pre‐filtering, the total number of markers used for the LA and HG populations were 2891 SNP and 7942 SNP, respectively. The SNP data for GWAS panel entries in all nurseries were called as a group and these data were imputed using BEAGLE with default parameters (version beagle.27Apr20.b81; Browning & Browning, 2007). GBS marker names are formatted listing the chromosome on which the marker is located followed by an underscore and the position in RefSeq Chinese Spring v1.0 (Appels et al., 2018).

Preliminary QTL analysis of the 2020 field trials in the LA population identified QTL on the distal ends of the long arms of chromosomes 2A (2AL) and 3A (3AL) that were of interest for further study. Additional markers were developed using kompetitive allele‐specific PCR (KASP) assays to increase marker density in these regions. Marker development targeted the 2AL and 3AL QTL by identifying new polymorphisms for the parent lines of the LA population covering a 10 Mbp region surrounding each QTL. The general position in RefSeq v1.0 was inferred from the markers flanking the QTL. Then, we searched and selected SNPs from exome capture data previously collected on the parents (triticeaetoolbox.org/wheat) to design KASP assays (Table S1). These newly developed KASP markers, as well as additional KASP markers flanking a powdery mildew locus on chromosome 6B and a KASP assay associated with the t1RS·1BL translocation, were evaluated in the LA population and the data were used in linkage map construction and QTL analysis.

sec.title: Linkage map construction
sec.p: Genetic linkage maps were produced for each of the RIL populations. Prior to linkage map construction, we removed low‐quality markers, defined as those markers with an excess of missing values (≥10%), segregation distortion (chi‐square test; α = 0.01), or co‐located markers with duplicated marker information. The genetic maps were constructed using the MSTmap (minimum spanning tree) algorithm on the R/ASMap package (Broman et al., 2003; Taylor & Butler, 2017; Wu et al., 2008). Clustering was achieved by estimating the recombination frequencies (r) between markers. When r = 0.5, the markers belong to two different linkage groups. Marker ordering and genetic distance in centimorgans were achieved by the traveling salesman path algorithm and the Kosambi mapping function, respectively. The overall genetic maps were visualized as density maps using the “LinkageMapView” R package (Ouellette et al., 2018).

sec.p: The phenotypic data were analyzed using a linear mixed model for categorical and continuous responses. For ordered categorical response data, we used a cumulative link mixed model (CLMM), a generalized linear mixed model with multinomial response distribution and cumulative logit link function to identify significant differences among genotypes (Christensen, 2018). Rank correlation coefficients (ρ) were calculated between all traits in all environments within each population using the R "cor" function with the Spearman method.

Following this, the restricted maximum likelihood method for continuous responses and maximum likelihood for categorical responses were used to estimate the best linear unbiased estimates (BLUEs) and variance components (Bates et al., 2015). The following mixed linear model was used:

Variance components were estimated using a complete random effects model. Their significance was tested through model comparison using likelihood ratio tests. Narrow‐sense heritability (h 2) was estimated following the approach suggested by Piepho and Mohring (2007).

sec.title: QTL mapping
sec.p: For each population, QTL analysis was performed for individual environments and using a combined model that included data from both environments in a mixed linear model with environment (location or year) as a random effect (see previous section). QTL analysis was performed using a composite interval mapping (CIM) approach with the “qtl” R package (Broman et al., 2003). For each trait, CIM was run using a window size of six and four covariate markers to provide a buffer in regions of the linkage map with low marker density for improved QTL detection. A significance logarithm of the odds (LOD) threshold was determined for an α = 0.05 using 1000 permutations for each trait; results significantly beyond this threshold are reported. The effects of each QTL on the phenotype were estimated using the Haley–Knott regression method. For each RIL population, QTL mapping results were visualized using the “LinkageMapView” R package (Ouellette et al., 2018).

Epistatic interactions among significant QTL detected in each of the mapping populations were modeled for both spike and leaf glaucousness traits in the combined‐environment QTL analyses. Epistasis was estimated as allele interaction effects in a multiple‐QTL model using the makeqtl() and fitqtl() functions in the R/QTL package. Allele interactions with F‐test p‐values < 0.05 were considered significant and reported.

sec.title: Genome‐wide association study
sec.p: The GWAS was conducted using phenotypic data from a panel of 176 wheat lines along with their genotypic information, which included 30,519 SNP. The analysis was performed using a memory‐efficient, visualization‐enhanced, and parallel accelerated “rMVP” R package (Yin et al., 2021). A fixed and random model circulating probability unification (FarmCPU) approach with a Bonferroni correction threshold of 0.05 was used to identify MTA. The population structure was captured using four principal components (principal component analysis = 4), which explained above 20% of the variation, and the kinship matrix. The kinship matrix was constructed from imputed data for all SNP using the VanRaden method (VanRaden, 2008). The assessment of disequilibrium between markers was measured as r 2 using rTASSEL (Monier et al., 2022).

sec.title: Field phenotypic analyses
sec.p: Across environments, the parents of each RIL population differed in glaucousness ratings (Figure 1A) and the trait segregated in the RIL progeny (Figure 1B). GA06493‐13LE6 had glaucous spikes (mean score = 3.9) and flag leaves (mean score = 3.9), while Hilliard had only mildly glaucous spikes (mean score = 1.0) and leaves (mean score = 1.0). For the LA population, parent AGS2000 had highly glaucous spikes (mean score = 4.0) and flag leaves (mean score = 4.0), while LA95135 had mildly glaucous spikes (mean score = 1.0) and flag leaves (mean score = 1.1). None of the RILs exhibited the non‐glaucous, or glossy, phenotype (rating of 0). However, a small number of non‐glaucous genotypes were given a 0 score in the GWAS panel. This resulted in a wider phenotypic range in the GWAS panel (Figure 1B).

Variation for both flag leaf and spike glaucousness was present in each of the populations (Figure 1B). A nonparametric (CLMM) approach was used to test for the significance of spike and flag leaf glaucousness, which were phenotyped as categorical ratings. Both exhibited significant differences for the combined analysis (chi‐square p‐value < 2.2e‐16) in all three populations (Table S2).

In each wheat population, Spearman's rank correlation coefficients (ρ) between spike and leaf glaucousness ratings were calculated using individual environment and multi‐environment means (Table S3). When combined means were considered, spike and flag leaf glaucousness ratings were moderately correlated, ranging from 0.47 in the elite line panel and 0.52 in each of the LA and HG mapping populations. Within a given environment, spike and flag leaf glaucousness ratings tended to be less correlated, with ρ as low as 0.28 in the KIN21 trial of the HG population. However, ratings of the same tissue type across environments were highly correlated for both leaf wax ratings (ρ = 0.62–0.69) and spike wax ratings (ρ = 0.64–0.79). This allows for improved power to detect QTL in multi‐environment trials.

Narrow‐sense heritability (h 2) estimates were calculated using variance components for spike and leaf glaucousness traits. For the GWAS panel, leaf glaucousness heritability was 0.82, and spike glaucousness heritability was 0.91. Estimates for RIL populations are as follows. Leaf glaucousness heritability was 0.84 and 0.85 for the HG and LA populations. Spike glaucousness heritability was 0.79 and 0.81 for the HG and LA populations. Spike glaucousness heritability was higher in the GWAS panel than in the RIL populations; estimates of leaf glaucousness heritability were consistent (h 2 = 0.82–0.85) in all three populations.

sec.title: Genetic linkage maps
sec.p: Genetic linkage maps were constructed for the HG and LA populations. The HG genetic linkage map encompassed 2830 cM with 1428 SNP markers (Table S4). The map comprised 19 linkage groups assigned to 18 wheat chromosomes (Figure S1). Of these, chromosome 7B has more than one linkage group, and 3D, 4D, and 5D were unable to be represented due to a lack of marker diversity on those chromosomes. This problem is fairly common in the wheat D genome, which has low allelic diversity, particularly for crosses between adapted cultivars or breeding lines. Although marker data from all 332 lines were used for linkage map construction to maximize resolution of the map, only 189 lines had sufficient seed for replicated, multi‐environment trials when phenotyped. Thus, the higher resolution in the map does not translate to higher power in the QTL analysis for this population.

All 21 wheat chromosomes were represented in the linkage map for the LA population. The LA population genetic map encompassed 4108 cM with 3408 SNP markers corresponding to 1881 loci (Table S4). This map comprised 26 linkage groups assigned to all 21 wheat chromosomes, of which chromosomes 1B, 4A, 5B, 6D, and 7A contained more than one linkage group (Figure S2). The genetic linkage maps provided sufficient marker coverage across the hexaploid wheat genome to serve as the groundwork for subsequent QTL analyses.

sec.title: Hilliard × GA06493‐13LE6 population QTL mapping
sec.p: Significant QTLs were detected in the HG RIL population for spike and flag leaf glaucousness traits in the combined analysis (Table 1). Additionally, the QTL mapping results from individual environments are reported in Table S5. For all QTLs reported, the allele associated with increased glaucousness is contributed by the GA06493‐13LE6 parent. The majority of flag leaf variation was explained by a QTL located on the distal end of the long arm of chromosome 3A, hereby named QFlg.ncb‐3A (120 cM). Functioning as the main driver of glaucousness in this population, QFlg.ncb‐3A accounted for 36.6% of the genetic variance of flag leaf glaucousness in the HG population.

sec.p: In the single location linkage analysis (Table S5), QFlg.ncb‐3A explained 32.9% and 23.8% of genetic variance in flag leaf glaucousness in Raleigh and Kinston, respectively. In the same genomic region, QSpg.ncb‐3A (123 cM) was identified as the primary determinant of spike glaucousness, explaining 21.2% of the variation for this trait in the combined location model (Table 1).

The QFlg.ncb‐3A and QSpg.ncb‐3A QTL have narrow confidence intervals of 3 cM based on CIM (Figure S3). Markers flanking the confidence interval of QFlg.ncb‐3A align to chromosome 3A positions 613,343,859–621,010,472 bp. This flag leaf QTL peaks between the first two markers in this region (positions 613,343,859–616,867,989 bp), where LOD = 22.2. The spike glaucousness QTL, QSpg.ncb‐3A, peaks near the S3A_616867989 marker and has a confidence interval flanked by markers at positions 613,343,859–628,712,890 bp. These co‐located QTLs on chromosome 3A may be due to a common variant, which is expected to be located somewhere within the 613.3–628.7 Mbp positions.

The second‐largest effect QTL for flag leaf glaucousness in the HG population was detected on chromosome 4B, explaining 11.6% of the variation for this trait (Table 1). This QTL, QFlg.ncb‐4B.1 (18 cM), mapped to a 3 cM confidence interval and peaked at position 565,312,655 bp. On chromosome 1A, two different regions were associated with flag leaf and spike glaucousness, respectively. Spike glaucousness QTL QSpg.ncb‐1A.1 (0 cM) was identified on the distal end of the short arm and explained 5.8% of the variation in spike glaucousness. In contrast, QFlg.ncb‐1A (84 cM), which explained 8.6% of the variation in flag leaf glaucousness, mapped to the long arm of the chromosome. The peak locus was flanked by markers at positions 520,868,230–531,680,970 bp. The confidence intervals of these QTLs are separated by over 70 cM and thus represent distinct regions that influence glaucousness on two different wheat tissues.

Two QTLs of interest detected in the HG population are associated with the flag leaf glaucousness trait on the short arms of chromosomes 2A and 2D (Figure S3). These QTLs, QFlg.ncb‐2A.1 and QFlg.ncb‐2D, map to the first 4 cM of the 2A and 2D linkage groups, respectively, and peak at the most distal marker of each linkage group. Notably, QFlg.ncb‐2D is located on the distal end of the short arm of chromosome 2D, where glaucousness genes Wax2 (W2) and Inhibitor of wax2 (Iw2) were previously identified (Tsunewaki & Ebana, 1999). QFlg.ncb‐2A.1, located in the distal region of the short arm of chromosome 2A, was found in a similar chromosomal region as the W2 locus on chromosome 2D, as well as the gene cluster W1 on chromosome 2B (Hen‐Avivi et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2017). However, a homoeologous wax locus similar to W1 and W2 identified on the other group 2 chromosomes has not been reported for chromosome 2A.

Interestingly, when mapping QTL for each location individually, these QTLs were each detected in only one location (Table S5). QFlg.ncb‐2D, explaining 7.3% of variation in flag leaf glaucousness, was detected in the KIN21 environment. QFlg.ncb‐2A was detected in the RAL21 environment. This suggests that environment may play a role in the relative influence of different genomic regions on the expression of glaucousness traits and our ability to detect their effects.

sec.title: Epistatic interactions among detected QTL
sec.p: Multi‐locus models using all QTLs detected for each glaucousness trait as model terms were used to test for epistasis; significant interactions (p ≤ 0.05) are reported in Table S6. Multiple significant epistatic interactions were detected among three flag leaf glaucousness QTL: QFlg.ncb‐1A, QFlg.ncb‐3A, and QFlg.ncb‐4B.1. These included a three‐way interaction (p = 0.028) between the three loci, as well as between the two pairwise interactions among QFlg.ncb‐1A and QFlg.ncb‐3A (p = 0.024) and QFlg.ncb‐3A and QFlg.ncb‐4B.1 (p = 0.014). No significant epistatic interactions were detected among spike QTL in the HG population.

Overall, QTL mapping in the HG population detected a single main driver of both flag leaf and spike glaucousness: the QFlg.ncb‐3A and QSpg.ncb‐3A QTL, respectively, both located at around 613–628 Mbp on the distal end of chromosome 3A. Furthermore, additional QTLs contributing significant influence on both traits were identified. Epistatic interactions were detected among leaf glaucousness QTL, with multiple involving QFlg.ncb‐3A. Our results in the HG population indicate a central role of QFlg.ncb‐3A in the genetic regulation of glaucousness in flag leaves and, to a lesser extent, spikes.

sec.title: LA population QTL mapping
sec.p: A combined environment model including 2 years of field trials at the Raleigh, NC, location and a large, phenotyped mapping population enabled identification of a large genetic contribution to spike and flag leaf glaucousness in the LA RIL population (Table 2). Results for individual environments (years) are given in Table S7. For all but one QTL (QFlg.ncb‐6B), the more glaucous allele is contributed by parent AGS2000.

sec.p: Similarly to the HG population, a QTL on chromosome 3A, QFlg.ncb‐3A (163 cM), was the primary genetic determinant of flag leaf glaucousness, explaining 30.5% of variation in the combined analysis (Table 1; Figure S4). What was different, however, was the relatively low contribution of this locus to spike glaucousness in the LA population, where it explained 9.1% of genetic variance in spike glaucousness. Instead, three QTLs not detected in the HG population contributed more significantly to spike glaucousness in the LA population.

The peak marker for the 3A QTL is called at neighboring markers for spike and flag leaf glaucousness. For leaves (QFlg.ncb‐3A), the peak marker is located at position 603,900,770 bp on chromosome 3A (Table 2; Appels et al., 2018). For spikes (QSpg.ncb‐3A), the peak marker is located at 602,018,522 bp.

The second‐largest contributor (percent variance explained [PVE] = 9.0) to flag leaf glaucousness in the LA population was QFlg.ncb‐2B (2 cM), located in a 7 cM confidence interval on the distal end of chromosome 2B (Table 2). The nearest markers to the QFlg.ncb‐2B align with the 9,713,222 bp position and its confidence interval is flanked by markers at the 2,416,524‐11,077,140 bp positions. The W1 locus was identified in this region, located from approximately the 3–5 Mbp positions of chromosome 2B (Hen‐Avivi et al., 2016). At a short distance proximally lies Iw1, another known glaucousness modulator (Huang et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2015). Genetic variants in these loci may be related to the flag leaf glaucousness variation from QFlg.ncb‐2B in the LA population.

Other loci contributing to leaf glaucousness include QFlg.ncb‐4B.2 (108 cM, PVE = 7.7), which was also detected in the HG population. The QTL, QFlg.ncb‐2A.2 (105 cM, PVE = 4.9), is located in the long arm of chromosome 2A, and its location is a significant distance distally to QFlg.ncb‐2A.1 that was detected on this chromosome in the HG population (Table 1). Thus, it appears to be distinct. Based on the overlapping confidence intervals for both spike and flag leaf traits, the QTLs found on chromosomes 2A, 3A, 4B, and 6B contribute to the expression of glaucousness in both tissue types in the LA population (Figure S4).

Unique to the LA population, three major QTLs were detected for spike glaucousness, each individually contributing greater influence than QSpg.ncb‐3A (Table 2). These were mapped to linkage groups 1B.1, 2A, and 4D, hereafter referred to as QSpg.ncb‐1B (1 cM), QSpg.ncb‐2A (74 cM), and QSpg.ncb‐4D (81 cM). For all three loci, the glaucous allele is contributed by parent AGS2000.

The most significant of these, QSpg.ncb‐1B, explains 22.8% variation in the LA population combined environment model. Notably, this QTL maps to the 1B.1 linkage group of the LA linkage map, which comprises the t1RS·1BL short arm chromosomal translocation from rye. QSpg.ncb‐2A contributed almost as much influence on spike glaucousness as QSpg.ncb‐1B, explaining 20.7% of variation. QSpg.ncb‐2A maps to a 6 Mbp region (734–739 Mbp) on the long arm of chromosome 2A, peaking at 737,386,570 and 738,782,799 bp. As noted above, this QTL also contributed, to a lesser extent, to flag leaf glaucousness. QSpg.ncb‐4D was detected in a 5 cM confidence interval peaking at 489,467,997 bp on chromosome 4D. QSpg.ncb‐4D explained 14.2% of variance in spike glaucousness (Table 2).

sec.title: Epistatic interactions among detected QTL
sec.p: Multi‐locus models identified significant epistatic interactions for spike and flag leaf glaucousness traits in the LA population. Significant epistatic interactions were detected among three flag leaf glaucousness QTL: QFlg.ncb‐2B, QFlg.ncb‐2A, and QFlg.ncb‐4B.2 (Table S6). These included a three‐way interaction (p = 0.050) between the three loci. Also, the pairwise interaction between QFlg.ncb‐2B and QFlg.ncb‐4B.2 (p = 0.039), which are a part of the three‐way interaction. None of these QTLs are the same as those QTLs detected as being part of epistatic interactions in the HG RIL population. Additionally, six spike glaucousness QTLs detected in the LA population were involved in multiple significant epistatic interactions: QSpg.ncb‐1A.2, QSpg.ncb‐1B, QSpg.ncb‐3A, QSpg.ncb‐4B, QSpg.ncb‐4D, and QSpg.ncb‐6B. These included many interactions among three loci (Table S6). Also, one four‐way interaction between QSpg.ncb‐1B, QSpg.ncb‐3A, QSpg.ncb‐4B, and QSpg.ncb‐6B was found (p = 0.014). Noteworthy QTLs involved in these epistatic interactions are QSpg.ncb‐3A, which coincides with the major flag leaf glaucousness QTL QFlg.ncb‐3A, and QSpg.ncb‐1B, which is linked to the t1RS·1BL alien introgression from rye. These results suggest epistatic interactions play a central role in the genetic control of spike and flag leaf glaucousness. Furthermore, our results in the LA population indicate that the t1RS·1BL alien introgression is involved in the epistatic control of spike glaucousness.

sec.title: Glaucousness genome‐wide association study
sec.p: Using the FarmCPU model, the most highly significant MTAs were detected on chromosomes 3A and 6B for flag leaf and spike glaucousness, respectively. The SNP at position 609,909,640 bp on the distal end of on chromosome 3A was most significantly associated with flag leaf glaucousness. The SNP at position 691,137,110 bp on the distal end of chromosome 6B was most significantly associated with spike glaucousness. These regions were also identified as significant QTLs in at least one of the RIL mapping populations.

Two MTAs associated with spike glaucousness were identified in chromosome 2B (Table 3); one on the distal end of the short arm (8,227,136 bp) and the other one more proximal (184,573,557 bp). The region of the MTA on the short arm (S2B_8227136) was also identified in the LA population. On the distal end of chromosome 1B (S1B_6823670), an MTA was significantly associated with spike glaucousness. Relatively high MAFs for the SNPs identified on chromosomes 4B, 2B, and particularly 3A (MAF = 0.36) indicate their accessibility in current breeding germplasm.

sec.p: An analysis of linkage disequilibrium (LD) in the 3A_609909640 QTL region among lines in the panel revealed variable correlations among GBS SNP in this region (Figure 2C). There was a mixture of markers showing markedly little LD with neighboring markers as well as correlated markers. No LD was observed between markers S3A_603900770 and S3A_613343859, which were identified as significantly associated with flag leaf glaucousness in the LA and HG mapping populations, respectively. The most significant marker in the GWAS, S3A_609909640, showed moderate LD with S3A_613343859 (r 2 = 0.25) and very little with S3A_603900770 (r 2 = 0.07). However, marker S3A_609909640 showed high LD with other SNP spanning the region from 602.8 to 605.9 Mbp (3A_602859969, S3A_603824966, S3A_603932976, S3A_605167769, S3A_605245073, and S3A_605990866). This suggests that detection of this MTA in a GWAS of regional germplasm likely represents the same locus or loci identified in the RIL populations.

sec.title: QTL mapping revealed distinct loci uniquely associated with spike glaucousness
sec.p: Trait mapping of glaucousness in both spike and flag leaf tissues detected relatively similar loci in the HG population (Table 1). However, these two tissues were associated with notably different loci in the LA population (Table 2). This tissue‐specific difference may be associated in part with the presence of the t1RS·1BL introgression from rye, which segregates in the LA population but not the HG RIL.

In the GWAS, an MTA on the short arm of chromosome 1B (S1B_6823670) was identified as significantly associated with spike glaucousness (Table 3). Similarly, a QTL (QSpg.ncb‐1B) is also associated with spike glaucousness in the LA RIL population (Table 2) that segregates for the t1RS·1BL translocation, indicating that QSpg.ncb‐1B QTL may be attributed to the presence of the rye genome in the wheat chromosome 1B. The spike MTA in the GWAS (S1B_6823670) does not appear to be linked to the t1RS·1BL translocation, as the two markers (S1B_6823670 and K1RS.6110) were in very low linkage (r 2 = 0.01) with each other in our panel (data not shown). In the LA population, the t1RS·1BL translocation was associated with increased glaucousness on spikes. The spike tissue specificity of QSpg.ncb‐1B in the LA population and the MTA in the GWAS (S1B_6823670) suggests that one or both may be related to variation of the Iw3 locus, also located on distal end of the short arm of chromosome 1B and previously reported to influence glaucousness of spike tissues (Dubcovsky et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2014). However, further study work is needed to determine this.

Two additional major‐effect QTLs were detected for spike glaucousness in the LA population: one on the long arm of chromosome 2A (QSpg.ncb‐2A) and the other on the long arm of chromosome 4D (QSpg.ncb‐4D). QSpg.ncb‐2A contributed almost as much influence on spike glaucousness as the t1RS·1BL translocation, explaining 20.7% of variation. QSpg.ncb‐4D explained 14.2% of variance in spike glaucousness (Table 2). Collectively, these QTLs (QSpg.ncb‐1B, QSpg.ncb‐2A, QSpg.ncb‐4D) present novel tissue‐specific variation of glaucousness in wheat. Our results indicate that spike and flag leaf glaucousness are not under the same genetic control in this population, revealing different loci associated to different degrees with each tissue.

sec.title: Major glaucousness locus on chromosome 3A is present in the US wheat germplasm
sec.p: A locus on the long arm of chromosome 3A, Qflg.ncb‐3A, contributed significantly to glaucousness in all three SRW wheat populations used in this study. The RIL mapping populations each had a highly glaucous parent; these lines, GA06493‐13LE6 and AGS2000, were both released by the University of Georgia breeding program, which often releases highly glaucous lines (J. Johnson, personal communication, 2023). In the GWAS panel of 2020 elite SRW breeding lines, the peak marker at this locus, S3A_609909640, was present in over one‐third of the genotyped lines (MAF = 0.36). This 36% MAF is the frequency of the glaucous allele in the wheat panel, showing that the glaucous allele is not uncommon in the US wheat germplasm. Repeated detection of a locus in this region in the elite panel and in the two biparental mapping populations suggests that this region of 3A is currently the main driver of flag leaf glaucousness in the SRW wheat germplasm.

This region of chromosome 3A was associated with both flag leaf and spike glaucousness in the RIL mapping populations. For flag leaf glaucousness, this region explained 36.3% of the variation in the HG population and 30.5% in the LA population (Tables 1 and 2). For spike glaucousness, this region explained 23.8% of the variation in the HG population and 9.1% in the LA population (Tables 1 and 2). Combining results from all populations presented herein, QFlg.ncb‐3A can be mapped to the region flanked by the markers at positions 602,028,522–616,867,989 bp on chromosome 3A (Figure 3).

sec.p: Loci in this 3AL region were also reported in two other glaucousness mapping studies in wheat that investigated global germplasm. Bennett et al. (2012) reported a major flag leaf glaucousness QTL in a biparental population of Australian wheat, located on chromosome 3A close to the simple sequence repeat marker Xwmc264. The position of this marker in RefSeq Chinese Spring v1.0 is at 625.8 Mbp, close to our reported QTL. Würschum et al. (2020) detected six significant MTAs in the 600–630 Mbp region of chromosome 3A in a GWAS of flag leaf glaucousness using a large global wheat panel. The most significant marker in Würschum et al. (2020), located at 3A_608499059, is quite close to the 3A_609909640 MTA identified in this study. While the relationship of the markers associated with significant loci identified in our populations and those identified by Würschum et al. (2020) is unclear, taken together these results point to a significant role of the 3A region on flag leaf glaucousness globally.

sec.title: Epistatic interactions contribute to the genetic control of glaucousness
sec.p: A growing pool of evidence suggests that epistatic interactions may play a major role in the genetic control of glaucousness. This includes multiple reports in the 3A QTL regions in our SRW wheat RIL mapping populations and a global wheat panel evaluated by Würschum et al. (2020). In this study, the authors found that one significant marker, D1095884 at ∼606 Mbp on chromosome 3A, had an epistatic interaction with the two closely linked markers at ∼621.5 Mbp detected on the same chromosome (Würschum et al., 2020). We find evidence for epistatic interactions involving QTL in this region of chromosome 3A with QTL on other chromosomes in both mapping populations (Table S6).

In the HG population, QFlg.ncb‐3A was found to be involved in significant epistatic interactions with two other leaf glaucousness QTL, QFlg.ncb‐1A and QFlg.ncb‐4B.1, both individually and as part of a three‐way epistatic interaction. The QFlg.ncb‐3A was not found to be involved in significant epistatic interactions in the LA population. However, this region was also associated with glaucousness in spikes, and this QTL, QSpg.ncb‐3A, was involved in multiple epistatic interactions involving three or more loci. These findings suggest that the 600–625 Mbp region of chromosome 3A includes loci that contribute significantly to leaf and spike glaucousness individually and as part of epistatic interactions with other loci on this and other chromosomes.

The LA population revealed multiple loci contributing to spike glaucousness, including three QTLs with LOD scores >10 (Table 2). Numerous significant epistatic interactions were detected in multi‐locus models of these QTLs (Table S6). These included primarily interactions between three loci. Also, one four‐way interaction between QSpg.ncb‐1B, QSpg.ncb‐3A, QSpg.ncb‐4B, and QSpg.ncb‐6B was found (p = 0.014). In addition to this interaction, the QSpg.ncb‐1B QTL, which is linked to the t1RS·1BL alien introgression from rye, is also involved in multiple epistatic interactions among three loci. These results suggest that a locus (or loci) present or absent in the t1RS·1BL alien introgression is involved in a complex genetic network that impacts glaucousness specifically in spike tissues. Relatively uncommon in SRW wheat germplasm, the t1RS·1BL alien introgression being represented in the LA mapping population provided a unique opportunity to study its impact on glaucousness. Our findings reveal novel epistatic interactions involving an alien introgression in wheat that contribute to tissue‐specific glaucousness variation in spikes.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: Climate change necessitates crop improvement. As climate zones are predicted to shift poleward, altering the distribution of productive agricultural areas, improved crop adaptation is of increasing importance (Anderson et al., 2020). Discovery of adaptive traits and alleles as candidates for selection is a critical first step in this crop improvement. Thus, improved understanding of glaucousness will accelerate breeding efforts for wheat adaptation.

Our results confirm the 600–620 Mbp region of chromosome 3A (QFlg.ncb‐3A) as a major driver of flag leaf glaucousness in wheat and provide the first report of its impact on spike glaucousness. Peak marker S3A_609909640 had an MAF of 0.36 in the GWAS panel nurseries. This indicates that the glaucous allele is prevalent in Eastern US regional SRW wheat germplasm. In conjunction with the development and deployment of a KASP marker for S3A_609909640 by the Eastern Regional Small Grains Genotyping Laboratory (USDA‐ARS), adaptive alleles can easily be deployed by marker‐assisted selection for public SRW wheat breeders of this region. Together, our results suggest that the QFlg.ncb‐3A QTL could rapidly be employed by breeders to increase flag leaf and, to a lesser extent, spike glaucousness in wheat. Further, we revealed novel epistatic interactions, some involving an alien introgression on chromosome 1B (t1RS·1BL), with tissue‐specific impact on glaucousness of the wheat spike. These findings will help to improve breeding efforts for regional adaptation while contributing to our understanding of the role of glaucousness in global adaptation of wheat to abiotic stress.

caption.p: A separate document, 13 pages, includes seven supplemental tables and four figures. Information for these tables and figures are listed below.

Supplemental Table S1. List of kompetitive allele‐specific polymorphism (KASP) marker assays used in this study. SNP names reflect the chromosome and position in reference genome Chinese Spring v1.0 (Appels et al., 2018). Each KASP assay includes a common primer (C1) and unique primers for the first allele (AL1) and second allele (AL2).

Supplemental Table S2. Summary of nonparametric ANOVA results for leaf and spike glaucousness traits using the combined environment datasets in the LA95135 × AGS2000 (LA) population, Hilliard × GA06493‐13LE6 (HG) population, and the soft winter wheat panel.

Supplemental Table S3. Summary of Spearman's correlations between all wax phenotypes and environments as well as multi‐environment means (multi). Correlations significant at p < 0.10 (*), p < 0.05 (**), and p < 0.01 (***) levels are reported for each soft winter wheat population: (A) A panel of US elite lines grown in 2020 (R20) and 2021 (R21) in Raleigh, NC; (B) The LA95135 × AGS2000 (LA) population, grown in Raleigh in 2020 (R20) and 2021 (R21); (C) The Hilliard × GA06493‐13LE6 (HG) population, grown in 2021 in Raleigh (R21) and Kinston (K21), NC.

Supplemental Table S4. Summary of genetic linkage maps generated for the (A) Hilliard × GA06493‐13LE6 (HG) recombinant inbred line (RIL) population and (B) LA96135 ×AGS2000 (LA) RIL population. Recombination frequencies were estimated in centiMorgans (cM) using the Kosambi mapping function.

Supplemental Table S5. Summary of flag leaf and spike glaucuousness QTL mapping results for the Hilliard× GA06493‐13LE6 mapping population. Kinston (KIN21) and Raleigh (RAL21) field trials were grown in North Carolina, USA in 2021. Marker names from GBS‐derived SNP denote their base pair position in reference genome assembly Chinese Spring RefSeq v1.0. In cases where the QTL peak was not located at a SNP marker, the name of the nearest left and right flanking SNPs are reported. Estimated allele effects are reported in reference to the GA06493‐13LE6 allele.

Supplemental Table S6. Summary of all significant (p < 0.05) epistatic interactions detected among quantitative trait loci (QTL) for spike or flag leaf glaucousness. A multi‐locus model including all significant QTL for each wax trait was used to test for epistasis in the Hilliard × GA06493‐13LE6 (HG) and the LA95135 × AGS2000 (LA) mapping populations.

Supplemental Table S7. Summary of flag leaf and spike glaucuoness QTL mapping results for the LA95135 × AGS2000 mapping population. Field trials were grown in 2020 (RAL20) and 2021 (RAL21) in Raleigh, NC. GBS SNP marker names denote their base pair position in reference genome assembly Chinese Spring RefSeq v1.0. In cases where the QTL peak was not located at a SNP marker, the name of the nearest left and right flanking SNPs are reported. Estimated allele effects are reported in reference to the AGS2000 allele.

Supplemental Figure S1. Density plots of genetic linkage maps for the Hilliard × GA06493‐13LE6 (HG) mapping population. Recombination frequencies were estimated in centiMorgans (cM) using the Kosambi mapping function.

Supplemental Figure S2. Density plots of genetic linkage map for the LA96135 ×AGS2000 (LA) mapping population. Recombination frequencies were estimated in centiMorgans (cM) using the Kosambi mapping function.

Supplemental Figure S3. Linkage groups with significant (logarithm of odds > 5) quantitative trait loci (QTL) for the Hilliard × GA06493‐13LE6 mapping population. QTL were detected using composite interval mapping of trait means calculated across two location‐year environments. Confidence intervals are colored for QTL for glaucousness of two tissue types: spike (orange) and flag leaf (green).

Supplemental Figure S4. Linkage groups with significant (logarithm of odds > 5) quantitative trait loci (QTL) for the LA96135 × AGS2000 mapping population. QTL were detected using composite interval mapping of trait means calculated across two location‐year environments. Confidence intervals are colored for QTL for glaucousness of two tissue types: spike (orange) and flag leaf (green).
